title: What are the built-in Java annotations — `@Override` (compile-time check), `@Deprecated` (with `forRemoval`/`since` in Java 9+), `@SuppressWarnings`, `@SafeVarargs`, `@FunctionalInterface` — and when should each be used?
shortTitle: What are the built-in Java annotations?

s1_definition.profdef: The core built-in annotations in the `java.lang` package instruct the compiler rather than the runtime. `@Override` asserts that a method overrides a supertype method, so the compiler errors if it does not, catching signature mistakes. `@Deprecated` marks an element as discouraged, and since Java 9 it carries `since` to say when it was deprecated and `forRemoval` to warn that it will be removed. `@SuppressWarnings` tells the compiler to silence named warning categories like unchecked or deprecation for a narrowly scoped element. `@SafeVarargs` asserts that a generic varargs method does not perform unsafe operations on its varargs array, silencing the heap-pollution warning. `@FunctionalInterface` declares that an interface has exactly one abstract method, so the compiler errors if someone adds a second, protecting its use as a lambda target.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of these as official stamps Rajesh's compliance office puts on documents to catch mistakes early. The override stamp says "this form is meant to replace an existing official form," and if there is no matching official form, the office rejects it, catching a typo in the form name. The deprecated stamp says "this old form still works but please stop using it, and here is when we flagged it and whether we plan to withdraw it." The suppress-warnings stamp says "I have reviewed this specific line and I accept this particular warning, stop nagging me here only." The safe-varargs stamp says "I promise this bundle-of-items form is handled safely." And the functional-interface stamp says "this form must have exactly one action, and the office will reject any attempt to add a second."
s1_definition.oneliner: The built-in annotations are compile-time safety stamps: Override verifies overriding, Deprecated discourages use, SuppressWarnings silences specific warnings, SafeVarargs vouches for generic varargs safety, and FunctionalInterface enforces a single abstract method.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The core built-in annotations in the `java.lang` package instruct the compiler rather than the runtime. `@Override` asserts that a method overrides a supertype method, so the compiler errors if it does not, catching signature mistakes. `@Deprecated` marks an element as discouraged, and since Java 9 it carries `since` to say when it was deprecated and `forRemoval` to warn that it will be removed. `@SuppressWarnings` tells the compiler to silence named warning categories like unchecked or deprecation for a narrowly scoped element. `@SafeVarargs` asserts that a generic varargs method does not perform unsafe operations on its varargs array, silencing the heap-pollution warning. `@FunctionalInterface` declares that an interface has exactly one abstract method, so the compiler errors if someone adds a second, protecting its use as a lambda target.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of these as official stamps Rajesh's compliance office puts on documents to catch mistakes early. The override stamp says "this form is meant to replace an existing official form," and if there is no matching official form, the office rejects it, catching a typo in the form name. The deprecated stamp says "this old form still works but please stop using it, and here is when we flagged it and whether we plan to withdraw it." The suppress-warnings stamp says "I have reviewed this specific line and I accept this particular warning, stop nagging me here only." The safe-varargs stamp says "I promise this bundle-of-items form is handled safely." And the functional-interface stamp says "this form must have exactly one action, and the office will reject any attempt to add a second."

**One line to remember:** The built-in annotations are compile-time safety stamps: Override verifies overriding, Deprecated discourages use, SuppressWarnings silences specific warnings, SafeVarargs vouches for generic varargs safety, and FunctionalInterface enforces a single abstract method.

sections.s2_technical:
`@Override` is placed on a method that is intended to override a method from a superclass or implement one from an interface. Its value is that the compiler verifies the override actually matches an inherited method signature, so if you misspell the name or get a parameter type wrong, you get a compile error instead of silently creating a new, unrelated method. For example annotating an overridden `equals(Object)` ensures you did not accidentally write `equals(MyType)`, which is a classic bug that breaks collections. You should put it on every method you intend to override; it documents intent and prevents regressions when a superclass changes.

`@Deprecated` marks a program element as one that should no longer be used, usually because it is dangerous or a better alternative exists. Since Java 9 it takes two elements: `since` to record the version where it became deprecated, and `forRemoval` which when true signals the element is slated for removal, turning the usual soft warning into a stronger one. For example `@Deprecated(since = "2.1", forRemoval = true)` on an old transfer method tells callers to migrate now. You pair it with the Javadoc `@deprecated` tag explaining the replacement. Use it when you must keep an element for backward compatibility but want to steer users to a new API.

`@SuppressWarnings` disables specific compiler warning categories for the annotated element, taking a string array of category names such as "unchecked", "deprecation", "rawtypes", or "unused". The best practice is to apply it on the narrowest possible scope, ideally a single local variable or method, and never on a whole class, because a broad suppression can hide genuine new problems. For example suppressing "unchecked" on one line where a cast from a legacy raw API is unavoidable, with a comment explaining why it is safe. Overusing it is a smell; each suppression should be justified.

`@SafeVarargs` addresses a specific generics-plus-varargs hazard. A varargs method with a generic parameter type creates an array of a generic type, which is not fully type-safe and triggers a potential heap-pollution warning. If you have verified the method only reads the varargs and does not store unsafe references, you annotate it with `@SafeVarargs` to assert safety and silence the warning. It can be applied only to methods that cannot be overridden, meaning static, final, or private instance methods, and to constructors. For example a helper that builds a list from a generic varargs is a typical safe case.

`@FunctionalInterface` is placed on an interface to declare that it has exactly one abstract method and is intended to be used as the target type of a lambda or method reference. The compiler then errors if the interface has zero or more than one abstract method, which protects the contract. Default and static methods do not count against the single-abstract-method rule. For example annotating a custom `TransferValidator` interface with a single `validate` method guarantees that no one accidentally adds a second abstract method that would break every lambda using it. A senior engineer notes that these annotations are almost entirely compile-time aids with retention that does not affect runtime behavior for Override, SuppressWarnings, and SafeVarargs, while Deprecated is retained and visible through reflection and tooling, and that disciplined use of Override and FunctionalInterface catches a surprising number of real bugs before they ship.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India evolved its transfer API and ran into exactly the problems these annotations prevent.

Problem 1 — a developer meant to override the base validation method but mistyped the parameter type, so it silently became a new method and the real validation never ran, allowing a bad transfer. This is exactly what @Override prevents by forcing a compile error when nothing is actually overridden.

Problem 2 — an old transfer method had to stay for backward compatibility but needed to be retired, so callers had to be steered to the new method with a clear since and a removal warning. This is exactly the role of @Deprecated with since and forRemoval.

Problem 3 — a legacy raw-typed integration forced one unavoidable unchecked cast, a generic varargs helper needed to vouch for its safety, and a single-method validator interface had to be protected from accidentally gaining a second method. These are exactly the roles of @SuppressWarnings narrowly scoped, @SafeVarargs, and @FunctionalInterface.

The code defines an `Account`, a `TransferValidator` functional interface, a `BaseValidator` and a `BalanceValidator` showing a correct @Override, a `TransferService` with a deprecated old method and a new method, a narrowly scoped @SuppressWarnings, and a @SafeVarargs helper. The demo validates and runs a transfer from Rajesh to Priya using a lambda for the functional interface.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh with a million, Priya with two hundred fifty thousand, a transfer amount of forty-five thousand, a legacy transfer of one thousand, and two fee amounts.

Step 1. A positive-amount validator is created as a lambda against the TransferValidator functional interface. Because that interface is annotated functional and has exactly one abstract method, the lambda binds cleanly, and the compiler would have rejected the interface if a second abstract method had been added.

Step 2. The BalanceValidator overrides BaseValidator's validate method, and the @Override annotation guarantees that the signature truly matches the inherited method. The demo runs both the positive validator and the balance validator, which both pass for a forty-five thousand transfer against a million balance.

Step 3. The new transfer method debits Rajesh and credits Priya by forty-five thousand, so Rajesh falls to nine hundred fifty-five thousand and Priya rises to two hundred ninety-five thousand, and the result is logged.

Step 4. The legacy transfer method is called. It is marked deprecated with a since of two point one and forRemoval true, so callers see a compiler warning, and at runtime it logs a warning and delegates to the new method, moving one thousand so Rajesh falls to nine hundred fifty-four thousand and Priya rises to two hundred ninety-six thousand.

Step 5. The SafeVarargs helper builds a list from two fee amounts passed as generic varargs. Because the method only reads the varargs and does not store unsafe references, the SafeVarargs annotation vouches for its safety and suppresses the heap-pollution warning, returning a two-element list.

Step 6. The demo logs the updated balances and the fee list, demonstrating each annotation's role, with the narrowly scoped SuppressWarnings shown on the legacy cast helper to silence only the unavoidable unchecked warning.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 19:16:20 [INFO] transfer 45000.00 SAV2001 -> CUR3001
2026-10-30 19:16:20 [INFO] Rajesh=955000.00, Priya=295000.00
2026-10-30 19:16:20 [WARNING] transferLegacy is deprecated; use transfer(...)
2026-10-30 19:16:20 [INFO] transfer 1000.00 SAV2001 -> CUR3001
2026-10-30 19:16:20 [INFO] fees = [50.00, 18.00]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ── @FunctionalInterface + lambda ──
  TransferValidator (1 abstract method) ◄── lambda (from,amt)->amt>0
       │ compiler rejects a 2nd abstract method
       ▼
  positive.validate(rajesh, 45000) = true

  ── @Override verified ──
  BaseValidator.validate(Account, BigDecimal)
       ▲ overrides (compiler checks signature matches)
  BalanceValidator.validate(...)  = balance >= amount → true

  ── new vs @Deprecated ──
  transfer(...)        → preferred path (no warning)
  transferLegacy(...)  → @Deprecated(since 2.1, forRemoval=true)
       │ compiler warns caller; runtime logs + delegates to transfer

  ── @SafeVarargs ──
  listOf(fee1, fee2) → generic varargs, READ only → List.of → [50.00, 18.00]

  ── @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") ──
  castLegacy(Object) → narrowly scoped silence of one unavoidable cast
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Built-in Annotations ═══

  ┌─ Design Decisions ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  @Override on every intended override (catches signature typos).│
  │  @Deprecated(since, forRemoval) to steer migration, + Javadoc.  │
  │  @SuppressWarnings on the NARROWEST scope, always justified.     │
  │  @SafeVarargs only on non-overridable methods that READ varargs.│
  │  @FunctionalInterface to lock a single-abstract-method contract.│
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Annotation roles (as prose) ────────────────────────────────
  @Override: compiler verifies the method overrides a supertype method.
  @Deprecated: discourage use; since/forRemoval (Java 9+); retained, reflective.
  @SuppressWarnings: silence named categories (unchecked, deprecation...).
  @SafeVarargs: assert generic-varargs safety (static/final/private/ctor).
  @FunctionalInterface: exactly one abstract method; lambda target.

  ── Class Diagram ───────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │   <<interface>>              │   │       TransferService     │
  │   TransferValidator          │   │ + transfer(...)           │
  │   (@FunctionalInterface)     │   │ + transferLegacy(...)     │
  │ + validate(Account,BigDec)   │   │   @Deprecated(2.1, remove)│
  │ + default and(...)           │   │ + listOf(T...) @SafeVarargs│
  └──────────────┬───────────────┘   │ + castLegacy @Suppress    │
                 │ implemented by     └───────────────────────────┘
                 ▼ (lambda)
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ BalanceValidator extends     │
  │ BaseValidator                │
  │ + validate(...) @Override    │  ← verified override
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. positive.validate(rajesh,45000) → true (lambda on functional iface)
  2. balance.validate(rajesh,45000) → @Override verified → true
  3. transfer(rajesh,priya,45000) → debit/credit
  4. transferLegacy(...) → @Deprecated warn → delegates to transfer
  5. listOf(fee1,fee2) → @SafeVarargs → List.of

  Contract for @Override validate:
    Pre:  signature must match BaseValidator.validate
    Post: compiler error if it does not override anything
    Benefit: prevents silent "new method" bugs on refactor
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The core built-in annotations live in java.lang and mostly instruct the compiler rather than the runtime. Override asserts that a method overrides a supertype method, so the compiler errors if it does not, which catches signature mistakes like a mistyped parameter type that would otherwise silently create a new, unrelated method. I put it on every method I intend to override, because it documents intent and protects against regressions when a superclass changes.

Deprecated marks an element as discouraged, and since Java 9 it carries a since element to record when it was deprecated and a forRemoval element to warn that it will be removed, which turns a soft warning into a stronger one. I use it when I must keep an element for backward compatibility but want to steer callers to a better API, and I pair it with a Javadoc deprecated tag naming the replacement. SuppressWarnings silences named warning categories like unchecked or deprecation, and I apply it on the narrowest possible scope with a justification, never on a whole class, because a broad suppression hides genuine new problems.

SafeVarargs addresses the generics-plus-varargs heap-pollution warning. When a generic varargs method only reads its varargs and does not store unsafe references, I annotate it SafeVarargs to assert that safety, and it is allowed only on methods that cannot be overridden, meaning static, final, or private instance methods, and on constructors. FunctionalInterface declares that an interface has exactly one abstract method and is meant as a lambda target, so the compiler errors if someone adds a second abstract method, which protects every lambda that uses it, while default and static methods do not count against that single-method rule.

In our transfer API evolution at National Bank of India, these annotations prevented real bugs. A developer once meant to override the base validation method but mistyped the parameter type, so it silently became a new method and the real validation never ran, which Override now catches at compile time. We kept an old transfer method for compatibility and marked it Deprecated with a since of two point one and forRemoval true to steer callers to the new method. We had one unavoidable unchecked cast against a legacy raw integration that we silenced with a narrowly scoped SuppressWarnings, a generic varargs fee helper that we vouched for with SafeVarargs, and a single-method validator interface that we locked down with FunctionalInterface so no one could accidentally break every lambda by adding a second abstract method.

---

keyPoints: @Override: compile-time check that method correctly overrides parent
@Deprecated: marks element as obsolete — compiler warns on use
@FunctionalInterface: ensures interface has exactly one abstract method
@SafeVarargs: suppress heap pollution warnings on varargs
